title: Tourist sites
legendIntro: Tap a dot for the name and what the place is. Names appear as you zoom in.
note: Shrines, temples, historic sites, gardens, museums and landmarks of Tokyo. Positions come from each place's Japanese Wikipedia page or the Geospatial Information Authority address search. Opening days are not given; check before a visit.
credit: Positions: Japanese Wikipedia (CC BY-SA) and the GSI address search (国土地理院).

features.name: Akasaka Hikawa Shrine
features.note: Former prefectural shrine in Akasaka and one of the ten Tokyo shrines. It is a quiet green site among the high-rise offices around it.

features.name: Asakusa Shrine
features.note: Shrine standing just east of the Sensō-ji main hall, also called Sanja-sama. It holds the Sanja Festival each May, a large neighbourhood event.

features.name: Atago Shrine
features.note: Shrine on a hill in Atago, said to have been founded on the order of Tokugawa Ieyasu. It honours the fire-protection deity of the Atago cult and is reached by a steep stone stair.

features.name: Hanazono Shrine
features.note: Shrine in the middle of Shinjuku's entertainment district. Its small grounds stand among bars and offices.

features.name: Hie Shrine
features.note: Mountain-king shrine in Nagatachō that hosts the Sannō Festival, one of the three great Edo festivals. Reached by a long stair or escalator up from the street.

features.name: Kameido Tenjin shrine
features.note: Shrine to Sugawara no Michizane in Kameido, nicknamed the Dazaifu of the east. It is known as a place students pray for success in studies.

features.name: Kanda Myōjin shrine
features.note: Formally Kanda Shrine, in Sotokanda close to Akihabara. It is the guardian shrine of the old merchant districts of Edo.

features.name: Meiji Jingū shrine
features.note: Shrine to Emperor Meiji and Empress Shōken, founded in 1920 inside a large forested park next to Harajuku. A quiet walk of several minutes separates the busy streets from the main hall.

features.name: Namiyoke Inari Shrine
features.note: Inari shrine in Tsukiji, close to the old fish market site. Its name means wave-warding, and it is a small local shrine for the market district.

features.name: Nezu Shrine
features.note: Shrine in Nezu, a former prefectural shrine and one of the ten Tokyo shrines. It is known for its azalea garden, which is the reason to come in spring.

features.name: Shinagawa Shrine
features.note: Shrine in Kita-Shinagawa, a former Tokyo ten-shrine member. It is also one of the Tōkai seven lucky gods shrines, honouring Daikokuten.

features.name: Tomioka Hachiman-gū shrine
features.note: Hachiman shrine in Fukagawa, also called Fukagawa Hachiman. It is the centre of the east-bank festival district and lies beside Fukagawa Fudōdō.

features.name: Ueno Tōshōgū shrine
features.note: Shrine to Tokugawa Ieyasu inside Ueno Park, often counted among the three great Tōshōgū shrines and richly decorated.

features.name: Yasukuni Shrine
features.note: Shrine in Kudan that honours people who died in national service since 1853. Its history and its link to the adjoining war museum make it central to modern Japanese memory debates.

features.name: Yushima Tenman-gū shrine
features.note: Shrine to the scholar Sugawara no Michizane, popularly called Yushima Tenjin. Students come to pray for exam success, and the grounds are known for plum blossoms.

features.name: Ōji Inari Shrine
features.note: Shrine in Ōji tied to the folk tale of the Ōji foxfires and the rakugo story The Fox of Ōji. It claims to head the Inari shrines of eastern Japan.

features.name: Ekōin temple
features.note: Pure Land temple in Ryōgoku, tied to the history of the Sumida riverside and its sumo district. A short walk from the Ryōgoku Kokugikan sumo hall.

features.name: Fukagawa Fudōdō temple
features.note: Tokyo branch of Narita-san Shinshō-ji, beside Tomioka Hachiman-gū. Fire rituals are the reason to visit this busy Fukagawa temple.

features.name: Gokoku-ji temple
features.note: Shingon temple in Ōtsuka with a large wooded precinct. It lies away from the main tourist routes.

features.name: Gōtoku-ji temple
features.note: Sōtō Zen temple in Setagaya, originally Rinzai. It is the place linked with the beckoning cat figures, and many small cats fill one corner.

features.name: Ikegami Honmon-ji temple
features.note: Head temple of the Nichiren sect in Ikegami, in the far south of the city. Its large precinct makes it the main Nichiren site in Tokyo.

features.name: Jindai-ji temple
features.note: Tendai temple in Chōfu, just west of the 23 wards, set among springs and woods.

features.name: Kan'ei-ji temple
features.note: Head temple of the Tendai sect in the Kantō region, founded by shogun Tokugawa Iemitsu. It was the Tokugawa family's funeral temple on the Ueno hill.

features.name: Kuhonbutsu Jōshin-ji temple
features.note: Temple in Okusawa, Setagaya, with nine Buddha statues in three halls, in a quiet residential area.

features.name: Nishiarai Daishi (Sōji-ji) temple
features.note: Shingon temple in Nishiarai known as the Kōya-san of the Kantō. A fair is held here on the 21st of each month.

features.name: Ryūsen-ji (Meguro Fudō) temple
features.note: Tendai temple commonly called Meguro Fudō, after its Fudō Myōō main image. It is one of the old Fudō temples around Edo.

features.name: Sengaku-ji temple
features.note: Sōtō Zen temple in Takanawa, one of the three Sōtō temples of Edo. It is best known as the burial place of the forty-seven rōnin.

features.name: Sensō-ji temple
features.note: The Kannon temple of Asakusa, reached through the Kaminarimon gate and the Nakamise approach street. It is described as the oldest temple in Tokyo.

features.name: Shibamata Taishakuten temple
features.note: Nichiren temple in Shibamata, formally Daikyōji. The approach street and the temple carvings give a view of old shitamachi life in the east of the city.

features.name: Tsukiji Hongan-ji temple
features.note: Tokyo branch of the Nishi Hongan-ji Pure Land temple. Its main hall has an unusual building style, unlike any other temple in the city.

features.name: Zenkoku-ji temple
features.note: Temple on the main street of Kagurazaka, beside the neighbourhood's stone-paved lanes.

features.name: Zōjō-ji temple
features.note: Pure Land temple in Shiba Park. It stands in front of Tokyo Tower, so old temple roofs and the modern tower share one view.

features.name: Akasaka Palace State Guest House
features.note: A palace used to receive state guests, with a main building designated a national treasure in 2009. The Western-style facade is the draw.

features.name: Bank of Japan main building
features.note: A Western-style bank building on the site of the old gold mint office, listed among Tokyo's fifty architectural heritage works. Viewed from outside.

features.name: Daiba Park (Shinagawa fort No. 3)
features.note: The surviving third of the sea forts built to guard against Black Ships. The only fort open to walk on.

features.name: Denmachō prison site (Jisshi Park)
features.note: The site of Edo's main prison, now partly Jisshi Park. It is a designated Tokyo historic site.

features.name: Edo Castle site (East Gardens)
features.note: The site where Ōta Dōkan built a castle in 1457 and the Tokugawa shoguns later ruled from. Walls and the stone base of the main keep remain in the palace grounds.

features.name: Eitai Bridge
features.note: A steel bridge over the Sumida River, designated an important cultural property in 2007.

features.name: Former Furukawa residence
features.note: The Furukawa family estate took its present form in 1919, with a Western mansion, rose garden and Japanese garden. Named a national place of scenic beauty.

features.name: Former Iwasaki residence
features.note: The main house of the Mitsubishi founding family, with buildings designated important cultural properties. Part of the Japanese-style wing survives beside the Western house.

features.name: Former Ministry of Justice building
features.note: A red-brick government building in Kasumigaseki, designated an important cultural property. It shows how Meiji-era state offices were built in Western style.

features.name: Jiyū Gakuen Myōnichikan
features.note: A school building from 1921, when Jiyū Gakuen was founded as a girls' school, now open to visitors.

features.name: Kachidoki Bridge
features.note: A rare surviving bascule bridge over the Sumida River. Its span has been locked since 1980.

features.name: Kira mansion site (Honjo Matsuzaka-chō Park)
features.note: A small park on the site of Kira Yoshihisa's house, where the forty-seven rōnin attacked in the Akō incident.

features.name: Kiyosu Bridge
features.note: A self-anchored suspension bridge of 1928 built in the rebuilding after the 1923 earthquake. Designated an important cultural property.

features.name: Kozukahara execution ground site
features.note: The Edo-period execution ground on the northern road out of the city, in use into the early Meiji years. A stone Jizō image stands here.

features.name: Meiji Seimei Kan
features.note: A Shōwa-period office building designed by Okada Shin'ichirō and his brother, designated an important cultural property. It faces the old Marunouchi business district.

features.name: Mitsui Main Building
features.note: The head office of the former Mitsui conglomerate, on the site of the Mitsukoshi merchant house. Also where Dan Takuma was assassinated in 1932.

features.name: National Diet Building
features.note: The seat of Japan's parliament, built as the Imperial Diet's new building in November 1936. Its symmetrical form around a central tower is clear from outside.

features.name: Nihonbashi bridge
features.note: The bridge over the Nihonbashi River that gives the district its name and was the starting point of Edo's main roads.

features.name: Nijūbashi bridge, Imperial Palace
features.note: The iron bridge to the palace main gate, in front of the open plaza. It is the standard view of the Imperial Palace; the palace grounds beyond are entered only by prior arrangement.

features.name: Nikolai-dō cathedral
features.note: The Holy Resurrection Cathedral, seat of the Orthodox Church in Japan. Named for the Russian priest Nikolai, who brought the faith to Japan.

features.name: Old Shimbashi Station site
features.note: The site of Japan's first railway terminal, in the Shiodome area.

features.name: Saigō Takamori statue, Ueno
features.note: The bronze statue in Ueno Park honouring the Meiji restoration leader Saigō Takamori (1828–1877). It is the best known of three Saigō statues.

features.name: Sakuradamon gate
features.note: A surviving outer gate of Edo Castle on the south-west side, once the start of the road to Odawara. Its two-part gate-yard layout is intact.

features.name: Seien Bunko, Asukayama
features.note: A library built in 1925 for Shibusawa Eiichi's 80th birthday, in the grounds of his Asukayama house.

features.name: Senju Ōhashi
features.note: A bridge over the Sumida River on National Route 4, at the old northern gate of Edo. The Edo-period post town Senju lies on its north bank.

features.name: Shinagawa-shuku
features.note: The first post town on the Tōkaidō out of Edo, one of the four Edo-period posting stations. The old road line survives as a shopping street.

features.name: Takanawa Ōkido remains
features.note: The stone base of the checkpoint gate at the southern entrance to Edo on the Tōkaidō. A national historic site since 1928.

features.name: Tayasumon gate
features.note: An Edo Castle gate inside Kitanomaru Park with a front gate and a gate tower set at a right angle. It is a nationally designated important cultural property.

features.name: Tokyo Memorial Hall, Yokoamichō Park
features.note: A memorial opened in 1930 for the unidentified dead of the 1923 earthquake, later also holding those of the 1945 air raids. About 163,000 victims are remembered.

features.name: Tokyo Station Marunouchi building
features.note: The red-brick station front facing the Imperial Palace, from the Taishō period. Worth seeing from the plaza for the facade and its dome rooms.

features.name: Yanaka Cemetery
features.note: A metropolitan cemetery with about 7,000 graves, including those of Shibusawa Eiichi, Yokoyama Taikan and Hatoyama Ichirō.

features.name: Yasuda Auditorium, University of Tokyo
features.note: The University of Tokyo's main auditorium, completed in 1925 after the earthquake interrupted building. Site of the 1969 student occupation.

features.name: Yushima Seidō
features.note: A Confucian temple built in 1690 under the fifth shogun Tsunayoshi, later the shogunate's academy. A marker calls it the birthplace of school education in Japan.

features.name: Zōshigaya Cemetery
features.note: A metropolitan cemetery of about 12 hectares in south Ikebukuro. A quiet walk among Meiji and later graves.

features.name: Ōkuma Auditorium, Waseda University
features.note: The landmark auditorium of Waseda University, the main hall of the campus founded by Ōkuma Shigenobu.

features.name: Chidorigafuchi
features.note: Stretch of the old Edo Castle moat lined with cherry trees, with a walkway and rowing boats on the water.

features.name: Hama-rikyū Gardens
features.note: Tidal-pond garden beside Tokyo Bay, once a shogunal and feudal-lord residence, with skyscrapers rising behind the pines.

features.name: Imperial Palace East Gardens
features.note: Public part of the former Edo Castle grounds, with surviving stone walls, guardhouses and open lawns in the middle of the city.

features.name: Inokashira Park
features.note: Park around a spring-fed pond with boats and wooded paths, on the western edge of the city.
lines: Mitaka / Musashino 三鷹市・武蔵野市

features.name: Institute for Nature Study
features.note: Preserved patch of woodland and marsh near Meguro, kept close to a natural state rather than landscaped.

features.name: Kiyosumi Garden
features.note: Pond garden ringed with rocks brought from across Japan; walkers cross the water on stepping stones.

features.name: Koishikawa Kōrakuen
features.note: Edo-period feudal-lord garden that blends Japanese and Chinese landscape ideas, set directly beside the Tokyo Dome area.

features.name: Kyū-Shiba-rikyū Gardens
features.note: Small early Edo-period pond garden close to Hamamatsuchō, quieter than the larger gardens nearby.

features.name: Mukōjima-Hyakkaen
features.note: Garden planted with seasonal flowers and plants chosen for Edo-period literary taste, in the old east-bank district.

features.name: Rikugien
features.note: Edo-period stroll garden laid out around a pond, designed to evoke scenes from classical Japanese poetry.

features.name: Shinjuku Gyoen
features.note: Large park combining Japanese, English and French garden styles, with a wide range of trees and a greenhouse.

features.name: Ueno Park
features.note: Large public park holding several major museums, a zoo, Shinobazu Pond and many shrines and temples.

features.name: Yoyogi Park
features.note: Wide park of lawns and tree-lined paths beside Meiji Jingū, used by local people for walks and gatherings.

features.name: Edo-Tokyo Museum
features.note: City history museum with full-scale Edo buildings and models; reopened after renovation on 31 March 2026.

features.name: Fukagawa Edo Museum
features.note: Rebuilt Edo-period streets of the Fukagawa district, with houses, shops and sounds you can walk through.

features.name: Ghibli Museum, Mitaka
features.ja: 三鷹の森ジブリ美術館
features.note: Museum of the animation studio Studio Ghibli, in Inokashira Park's wooded edge.

features.name: Japan Folk Crafts Museum
features.note: Museum of everyday handmade objects from Japan and elsewhere, founded by the mingei movement.

features.name: Miraikan
features.note: National science museum on the Odaiba waterfront, with exhibits on robots, space and the earth.

features.name: Mori Art Museum
features.note: Contemporary art museum high in the Roppongi Hills tower, with views over the city.

features.name: Museum of Contemporary Art Tokyo
features.note: Large museum of postwar and contemporary art in Kiba, near Kiyosumi.

features.name: National Museum of Nature and Science
features.note: Natural history and science museum in Ueno Park, with fossils, specimens and a large dinosaur hall.

features.name: National Museum of Western Art
features.note: Western art collection in a building designed by Le Corbusier, listed as a World Heritage site.

features.name: Nezu Museum
features.note: Collection of pre-modern Japanese and East Asian art, with a large garden behind the galleries.

features.name: Shitamachi Museum
features.note: Museum of everyday life in the old lower-town districts, beside Shinobazu Pond. It has reopened after a period of closure.

features.name: Sumida Hokusai Museum
features.note: Museum devoted to the woodblock artist Hokusai, who was born in this part of the city.

features.name: The National Art Center, Tokyo
features.note: Large exhibition hall with a curving glass wall, holding changing shows rather than a permanent collection.

features.name: Tokyo Metropolitan Teien Art Museum
features.note: Former princely residence in Art Deco style, shown as an interior with a garden around it.

features.name: Tokyo National Museum
features.note: The national museum in Ueno Park, with the main national collection of Japanese art, swords, ceramics and archaeological finds.

features.name: Ōta Memorial Museum of Art
features.note: Museum specializing in ukiyo-e woodblock prints, in the Harajuku area.

features.name: Ameyoko market street
features.note: Crowded market street under and beside the rail tracks between Ueno and Okachimachi, selling food and goods.

features.name: Golden Gai
features.note: Tiny alleys of narrow bars in Kabukichō that survive from the postwar market period.

features.name: Kabuki-za theatre
features.note: Main kabuki theatre in Tokyo, in Ginza, in a building with a traditional-style roof.

features.name: Kappabashi Dougu Street
features.note: Street of shops selling kitchen tools, tableware and the plastic food models used in restaurant windows.

features.name: Rainbow Bridge
features.note: Suspension bridge across Tokyo Bay to Odaiba, with a walkway for pedestrians.

features.name: Ryōgoku Kokugikan
features.note: Sumo arena in Ryōgoku, which holds the main tournaments in Tokyo and has a small sumo museum.

features.name: Shibuya Scramble Crossing
features.ja: 渋谷スクランブル交差点
features.note: Crossing in front of Shibuya Station where traffic stops in all directions and pedestrians cross at once.

features.name: Shibuya Sky
features.note: Open-air rooftop observation deck on top of Shibuya Scramble Square, overlooking the crossing.

features.name: Takeshita Street
features.note: Narrow pedestrian street at Harajuku known for young people's fashion and snacks.

features.name: Tokyo Metropolitan Government Building
features.note: Twin-towered government headquarters in Shinjuku with public observation decks over the west of the city.

features.name: Tokyo Skytree
features.note: Broadcasting tower and the tallest structure in Japan, with observation decks above the east-bank districts.

features.name: Tokyo Tower
features.note: Red-and-white steel broadcasting tower with observation decks, a reminder of the 1950s postwar rebuilding.

features.name: Toyosu Market
features.note: The city's main fish and produce wholesale market, with a public viewing gallery above the tuna auction floor.

features.name: Tsukiji Outer Market
features.note: Market streets that remain on the site of the old wholesale market, mainly food stalls and shops.

features.name: Yanaka Ginza
features.note: Small shopping street in the old Yanaka district that keeps a local, low-rise townscape.
